title: Attracting foreign capital needs more than tax cuts
syllabus: GS3 › Indian economy and issues relating to mobilisation of resources; Investment models; Effects of liberalisation on the economy · GS4 › Fairness and impartiality in public policy
summary: With foreign portfolio investors pulling money out of Indian equities, the editorial argues that capital gains tax cuts alone will not bring them back; India needs a competitive regulatory and tax framework, without discriminating against domestic investors or curbing outflows.
ideas: Global pull factors, not just tax: capital is chasing companies across the AI value chain, where India has no significant presence, while rising US bond yields raise the risk-free return.
FPI outflows reflect global shifts, AI-led allocation and higher US yields, more than India's tax rates.
Valuations and earnings matter: corporate earnings expectations and high valuations also drove investors out, so tax concessions cannot be the main driver of market performance.
Tax cuts cannot fix markets where earnings growth and valuations fail to justify the price.
Compete as a jurisdiction: to attract capital and become a global financial centre, India needs a regulatory and tax framework competitive with friendlier jurisdictions.
Predictable regulation and a competitive tax regime, not one-off sops, make a country a global financial centre.
Some steps taken: in June the government exempted interest income and capital gains and eased norms to draw foreign investors into government bonds.
Opening government bonds to foreign investors widens the pool of finance for the state.
Fairness and openness: favouring dollar investors over rupee investors would be discriminatory, and curbing Indians' outward remittances to hold capital in would be a step backwards.
Policy for foreign capital must stay fair to domestic investors and keep India open in both directions.

practice.q: "Tax incentives alone cannot make India a preferred destination for global capital." Discuss with reference to recent foreign portfolio outflows.
parts: Role and limits of tax incentives

answer.t: Foreign portfolio investors have pulled large sums out of Indian equities since 2024-25, prompting calls to cut capital gains tax; the Finance Minister has cautioned that tax is not the main driver of markets.

pts.t: Global capital is flowing to companies across the AI chain, where India has little presence.
pts.ex: Nvidia, Google, Samsung, SK Hynix, TSMC.

pts.t: Higher returns on US bonds raise the risk-free rate and pull money back to developed markets.
Indian stocks priced high relative to earnings growth lose appeal.
Wars, tariffs and protectionism make investors cautious about emerging markets.
A weakening rupee cuts dollar returns for foreign investors.
Past episodes such as retrospective taxation (2012, repealed in 2021) still shape perceptions of risk.

answer.h: Role and limits of tax incentives

pts.t: Exemptions can tilt decisions in targeted areas.
pts.ex: June exemptions to draw foreign investors into government bonds.

pts.t: No tax cut compensates for weak earnings or a missing AI ecosystem.
Concessions reduce revenue without assured inflows.
Favouring dollar over rupee investors breaks tax neutrality.
Competing on tax alone invites a contest that small, low-tax jurisdictions win.
Simple, stable rules comparable to leading financial centres.
pts.ex: GIFT City IFSC as a test bed.

pts.t: Semiconductors, data centres and AI firms give investors India-linked AI exposure.
Inclusion and easier access widen stable, long-term foreign participation.
Encourage FDI and long-term funds over hot money.
Avoid retrospective or sudden changes in tax and rules.
Do not curb outward remittances under the LRS; openness signals confidence.

answer.t: Capital follows growth, predictability and technology; India wins it back by being a competitive, fair and open jurisdiction, not by tax cuts alone.
